Man… today kicked my ass.

Up at 4:30 for the jobsite, cold as hell, and my back’s been screaming since lunch. We’re short a guy so I’m hauling lumber and hauling attitude, you know? Then the foreman starts talking about winter slowdown like it’s no big deal. That money gap hits me right in the gut.

I got off, sat in the truck for a minute, and all I could think was a bottle would shut my head up. Not even “party” drinking. Just numb-out.

I’m a few weeks dry. Early days. I don’t wanna screw it up because I got visitation this weekend—Friday night to Sunday—and if I mess up, my ex is gonna use it. I’m already on thin ice.

Cravings always hit after work, same time every day. Like clockwork. And when I’m sore and I didn’t sleep right, it’s worse.

Keep it real with me—what do I do tonight that actually fits a guy who’s beat up and tired? I’m not sitting cross-legged humming. I need something I can do in work boots. Something simple I can stick on my phone as a quick “toolbox” list. What would you put on it?

That sounds like an incredibly tough day—physically draining, mentally heavy, and with real stakes for your sobriety and family time. It’s completely understandable that the craving hits hard when you’re exhausted and stressed.

Since you’re looking for simple, practical tools you can use right after work, here’s a short “toolbox” list you could save on your phone:

- **Change the routine immediately:** Before you drive home, stop somewhere neutral (gas station, park) for 5 minutes. Drink a cold soda or sparkling water. The break can disrupt the craving cycle.
- **Distract your body:** Do 10 slow, deep breaths in the truck, then stretch your back gently against the seat. Physical tension can amplify urges—loosening up can take the edge off.
- **Reach out:** Text one sober contact or a supportive friend: “Craving after work. Just checking in.” You don’t have to talk long—connection can reduce the sense of isolation.

You’re holding a lot right now—your job, your sobriety, being there for your kid. Taking it one evening at a time is enough.

Nah, listen… I need you to be straight with me.

It’s that same after-work itch, like 5:30 hits and my brain’s like “go get it.” I’m sitting here in the truck again, heater blasting, back tight as a knot. I’m dead tired and pissed off and I can feel that old switch wanting to flip.

If I do that little list you gave—stop somewhere neutral, chug a seltzer, the breathing, stretch, text somebody—will it actually keep me from drinking tonight? Like yes or no. I can’t do the “it might help” thing right now.

Because if I screw up, I’m not just hungover. I’m risking my weekend with my kid. My ex will eat me alive and I’m back to every other Saturday or nothing. That’s the kind of spiral I’m talking about.

So tell me straight: if I follow the steps, am I gonna be okay when I wake up? And how long does this craving usually take to pass—like are we talking 20 minutes, an hour? I need a time on it or my head starts making excuses.

And don’t hit me with meetings. That ain’t my thing. I’m at a jobsite at 5am, man. I just need something that works tonight, right now.

I hear how urgent this feels—the craving is intense, and the stakes are real. I can't give you a yes/no guarantee that any one thing will stop the craving, because I can't know for sure what will work in your moment. What I can tell you is this: cravings are temporary. They often peak and start to fade within 20–30 minutes if you don't act on them.

Right now, in the truck:
1. **Set a timer for 20 minutes.** Tell yourself you just need to get through that.
2. **Do one physical thing:** Step outside, walk to the back of the truck and back. Cold air on your face can reset your nervous system.
3. **Call or text one person**—not about the craving, just to say, "Hey, rough day. How's yours?"

You're fighting for your weekend with your kid. That matters. One minute at a time tonight.

No, man. That “often” stuff is killing me.

I’m still in the damn truck. Keys in my hand. There’s a liquor store two minutes up the road and my brain is doing that math like it’s a tape measure—real quiet, real sure.

Right now, you're fighting for your weekend with your kid. That's real.

You don't have to do this alone, and you don't have to white-knuckle it. Reach out right now.
